notes.title: On January 1, a federal tax credit starts paying for tutoring. No university prepares tutors for it.
notes.standfirst: The new federal scholarship tax credit can cover tutoring and after-school programs for public school students, not only private tuition. Thirty-one states have opted in. The workforce it pays for has no degree path.
body: The federal scholarship tax credit created in 2025 takes effect on 1 January 2027. Taxpayers get a dollar-for-dollar federal credit of up to $1,700, or $3,400 for married couples, for donating to scholarship-granting organizations. As of 14 October, 31 states had opted in, three governors had declined and 16 governors plus the mayor of the District of Columbia had not decided.

The scholarships are not only for private tuition. They can also cover public school students' expenses such as tutoring and after-school programs. The IRS projects the program could reach $26 billion in 2030 in the 30 states that opted in before 1 October, serving at least 2 million students. Michigan State's Josh Cowen, a critic of the program, estimates about $3.2 billion of it could reach public school students.

That money pays tutors, coaches and after-school staff: the roughly 4 million people Arizona State's education college now calls the youth-serving workforce. In the 102-university scan, ASU's push to build credentials for that workforce is the only one we found.

The limit, first. The IRS has not published the final list of allowable expenses and calls it a high priority. How much of the money reaches tutoring, rather than tuition, is unknown until donors give and organizations spend. This note records a new funding stream and an empty preparation pipeline, not a shortage.

What to watch. Whether any college of education builds a tutoring or youth-work credential aimed at scholarship-funded providers in 2027, and whether scholarship organizations set any qualifications for the tutors they pay.

sources.label: Education Week — Democratic holdouts still aren't committing to the federal program (14 Oct 2026)

notes.title: Who prepares the teachers of microschools, classical schools and Christian schools? Mostly organizations that publish no counts.
notes.standfirst: We found twelve organizations preparing educators for the schools portable funding pays for. Three publish a number of people prepared. One reports to a state.
body: Our Florida supply data counts only people who finish a state-approved program. Teachers in private schools and microschools usually need no state certificate, so their preparation is invisible to the state, to Title II and to IPEDS. We went looking for it directly.

Microschools. The Micro Schools Network sells a $3,500 leadership certificate that bundles Harvard's general Instructional Leadership Certificate with its own microschool course. ASU Prep runs a Microschool Entrepreneur Fellowship. KaiPod Catalyst's first founder cohort had 17 people from 13 states, 80% of them former classroom teachers. The National Microschooling Center launched a training institute in 2026. Prenda said in 2021 that about 30% of its guides were certified teachers; its Florida page now says about half. Acton Academy reported 250+ affiliate schools in 2021 and publishes no guide-training figures.

Classical schools. Hillsdale College's Graduate School of Classical Education opened in 2022 with 11 master's students and aimed for 15–20 a year. Great Hearts runs an Academy for Classical Teachers and publishes no counts.

Christian and Montessori schools. ACSI certifies Christian-school teachers with a bachelor's degree in any field plus Bible and philosophy-of-education requirements; it publishes no count of holders. Florida's FACCS certification “stands alongside” state certification. The National Center for Montessori in the Public Sector now has 11 affiliated teacher education programs.
Only one provider appears in a state count: Noble Education Initiative, whose online program finished 116 Florida teachers in 2023–24 because it is state-approved.

The limit, first. This is a list, not a census. Absence of a published count is not absence of training. The finding is narrower: the preparation that serves this sector is real, scattered, mostly outside universities, and mostly uncounted.

notes.title: On the ESA vendor lists, universities are a rounding error.
notes.standfirst: Texas lists 5,648 approved vendors for its new ESA program. About ten belong to colleges, and most of those are campus child-care centers.
body: We searched every public ESA provider list we could find for colleges and universities: Texas, Alabama and Utah. Arizona and Florida keep their marketplaces behind a login.

Texas. The Education Freedom Accounts vendor finder lists 5,648 entries across eight vendor types. College-linked entries: UT Austin's online UT High School, campus child-development centers at UT Austin, UT Rio Grande Valley and SMU, community-college early childhood centers, and Stephen F. Austin State University for enrichment.

Alabama. The CHOOSE Act provider list, dated 23 October 2026, has about 1,400 entries. Roughly ten are colleges. Auburn appears as an online K–12 private school and a course provider; the University of South Alabama offers dual enrollment and a literacy center.

Utah and Arizona. BYU's independent-study high school courses take Utah Fits All funds. In Arizona, ASU Prep Digital is an approved vendor, and about 0.7% of ESA spending reaches any postsecondary institution.

The limit, first. A vendor listing shows availability, not spending. We could not see how much ESA money any college received, except Arizona's aggregate. Universities may also be paid indirectly, through dual enrollment arranged by a school.
What it shows. Where universities sell directly to ESA families, they sell K–12 schooling, courses and pre-K child care. None of the listings is a preparation program for educators.

notes.title: Nine campus centers study the new schools. None prepares their teachers.
notes.standfirst: Research on hybrid schools, homeschooling and microschools now has a home on campus. Preparing the people who teach in them does not.
body: We checked nine university centers that study school choice or the schools it pays for, against six things a center can do: study, publish data, convene, train researchers, prepare educators, and run schools.
All nine study. Four publish data. Three convene. Two train researchers: Harvard's PEPG and Arkansas's Department of Education Reform. None prepares educators, and none runs a school.

The newest models get studied from unexpected places. Kennesaw State's National Hybrid Schools Project sits in its business school, not its education college. Johns Hopkins's Homeschool Hub publishes participation data for 39 states. Tulane's federally funded choice center closed when its award ended in August 2025. Michigan State's EPIC, once a partner in that center, now studies the educator workforce instead of choice.

The limit, first. Nine centers is a starting set, not a census. A blank means the activity was not documented, not that it never happens. Funders appear on every side: EdChoice, Walton and Windgate for some centers; the NEA and AFT for Colorado's NEPC.
The full table, with each center's funding and source, is on the Leaders page.

notes.title: Arizona funds families to choose private schools. Its teacher scholarship does not count private-school teaching.
notes.standfirst: More than 100,000 students use Arizona's ESA. The state's own tuition-free teacher program requires graduates to teach in a public or charter school.
body: Arizona's Empowerment Scholarship Account program served 102,891 students in early 2026. Families can spend it on private tuition, tutoring and more.

The Arizona Teachers Academy waives tuition for future teachers at ASU, Northern Arizona, the University of Arizona and community colleges, about $15 million a year from the general fund. Recipients must “teach in an Arizona public or charter school” for each year of support. Private-school teaching does not count.

So the state pays for families to choose private schools, and pays for teachers on the condition that they do not work in one. Our October pass of Arizona's universities found the same shape: UA and NAU build preparation with districts, and ASU's choice-sector work sits in its K–12 arm, not its education college.

The limit, first. A scholarship rule does not determine where teachers go after their service ends, and private schools in Arizona can hire uncertified teachers. This note records a design choice in two state programs, not its effect.
Why it matters. Arizona has the largest universal ESA in the country. Its teacher pipeline policy was written before the money became portable, and it has not changed.

notes.title: A university-run school that turns down the voucher money.
notes.standfirst: Nova Southeastern's own PreK–12 school says state scholarships would limit its independence. It is the first documented refusal in the Index.
body: NSU University School, a PreK–12 school of about 1,850 students in Davie, describes itself as “an academic center of Nova Southeastern University.” Its tuition page states: “NSU University School does not participate in any state scholarship, grant, or voucher programs. These programs make the school vulnerable to restrictions and reporting requirements that limit operational independence.”
Florida has the largest scholarship programs in the country. A university that already runs a private school chose not to take that money, and said why.

The same university once built a charter-school master's degree and no longer offers it. The Index records both as Tier 0: an institution that built for the sector and stopped, and one that runs a school and declines the funding.

The limit, first. A school that refuses scholarships still serves families who chose it, and the decision belongs to the school, not the education college. We have not asked NSU when the policy began or whether it has been debated.
Why it matters. Most of this Index records absence. This is a documented choice, with a stated reason, by a university in the state that funds choice most.

notes.title: We said 70 universities showed no response. We had searched the wrong building in 17 of them.
notes.standfirst: A second search, outside the education schools, found universities running, founding or authorizing K–12 schools. The share with no response fell from about two in three to about half.
body: Our first pass of the 102 universities read mostly education-school pages. Correction 03 showed that misses what universities do elsewhere, so we searched every “none” row again: K–12 units, online schools, charter offices, lab schools and outreach centers.

Seventeen of 70 had a documented response. Twelve run, founded or authorize schools. UT Austin runs a 24-campus charter district and UT High School, an online public high school of 6,000+ students that now sells courses to Texas ESA families. UC San Diego operates the Preuss School. USC's Hybrid High grew into a six-school charter network. WashU authorizes KIPP St. Louis. Rutgers–Camden's LEAP Academy serves about 1,500 children. UNC–Chapel Hill runs its own lab school as its own school district.

Four more work with districts: Rochester ran East High for the city district until June 2025; UVA and JMU run new lab schools with their districts; Arizona builds teacher pathways with Sunnyside. One, RIT, partners with a charter high school.

What changed. No response found is now 46% of AAU members and 55% of the Most Innovative. We also withdrew our claim that responses sit mostly outside education schools; the recoded schools are split. Each recoded row is marked in the data, and the change is logged as Correction 04.

What did not change. None of the 17 prepares educators for microschools, hybrid schools or homeschool co-ops. The most common university response is still running or authorizing a school, not preparing anyone to teach in one.
The limit, first. UC Davis, Howard and Miami remain unresolved, and the first pass coded district partnerships unevenly; that needs its own pass.

notes.title: Florida's largest teacher preparer is not a university.
notes.standfirst: Florida's colleges and universities finished 60% fewer new teachers in 2023–24 than in 2010–11. District and charter programs held steady, and now finish more than any single university.
body: Federal Title II data count everyone who finishes a Florida state-approved program leading to a teaching certificate. In 2010–11, colleges and universities finished 7,406. In 2023–24 they finished 2,958. The State University System alone fell from 4,428 to 1,746.

District and charter programs did not fall. The state's Professional Learning Certification Program, run by districts, charter schools and charter management organizations, finished 652 teachers in 2010–11 and 657 in 2023–24. That makes it Florida's largest single preparer. The largest university, UCF, finished 392.

Private providers outside colleges went from none to 162. One of them, Noble Education Initiative, which serves more than 100 charter schools, finished 116 Florida teachers. The University of Florida finished 106. Programs outside colleges now produce 22% of Florida's new teachers, up from 8%.

Degrees fell less than certificates. Florida education bachelor's degrees fell 36% from 2011–12 to 2023–24. FIU awarded 433 education bachelor's degrees in 2023–24; 65 people finished its teacher program.

Added 31 October 2026: the timing. Most of the college decline came before portable funding reached most Florida students. College completers fell to 3,453 by 2022–23, the last year before HB 1 made every student eligible: 89% of the total drop. The whole pipeline fell 53%. These numbers show who prepares Florida's teachers now. They do not show that choice policy caused the shift. See Correction 05.

The limit, first. These counts include only programs leading to a Florida certificate. Private-school and microschool teachers who need no certificate, and Floridians trained by out-of-state online programs, do not appear. Neither source records where completers go on to teach. The 2016–17 federal file double-counts and is left out.
The chart and data are on the homepage.

notes.title: A Florida district needed a school model. It bought one from a microschool operator.
notes.standfirst: Polk County contracted a private microschool founded by two teachers who had left a Polk County public school. The Index has coded 21 Florida institutions and found no education-school program built for this sector. Both facts describe the same state in the same year.
body: This Index's Florida finding is an absence: the most portable education money in America, and no education-school program built for the sector it funds. This note records what filled that absence in one district.

In 2025 the Polk County school board unanimously approved a two-year contract with WonderHere to bring its microschool model into Philip O'Brien Elementary. WonderHere was founded in 2016 by two teachers who had left a Polk County public school. It now runs a state-approved private school of roughly 120 full-time students, plus about 300 students in weekly homeschool enrichment, with additional locations in Florida and South Carolina. Its founders have said since the beginning that their aim was to influence public education.

A public district bought instructional design and staff training from a private microschool operator. It did not buy them from a college of education, a state research arm, or a regional service agency.

The sourcing pattern is not confined to Florida. Elizabeth City-Pasquotank Public Schools in North Carolina — about 4,800 students, roughly 70% economically disadvantaged — opened a 26-student middle-grades microschool where students help run an Airbnb and learn with AI tutoring. The design came from visits to more than 40 schools, including private microschools in Texas. The staffing arithmetic is why design was the binding problem: three teachers and one support staffer are meant eventually to cover four grade levels and about 65 students. Superintendent Keith Parker put it plainly — three people are not going to be able to teach four grade levels.

The limit, before the conclusion. One contract and one out-of-state case are not a pattern. We have not established that any Florida college of education declined this work, was approached, or knew it was available. We have established only where two districts went. Neither school has achievement data, and this note makes no claim about whether either model works. Florida is a systematic pass in the 2026 baseline, but Field Note 06 records that 25 Florida state colleges remain unscanned. A program could exist that we have not found.

What it does establish is a dated demand signal. Districts in the state with the most portable funding in the country are purchasing school-model design on the open market. Somebody is being trained and paid to do that work. Identifying who — and whether any postsecondary institution is among them — is a supply-and-workforce question rather than a program-catalog one, which is the seam this Index was built to watch.

notes.title: Three-quarters of Florida districts now sell to students they do not enroll
notes.standfirst: District participation in Florida's part-time scholarship marketplace went from roughly one in three to about 75% of 67 districts in twelve months. Texas districts, offered state money for a comparable arrangement, mostly declined. The contrast is the finding.
body: The limit, before the conclusion. These are participation counts, not revenue. No Florida district has published what it earns from this channel, and a district can be an approved provider with two listed courses and no students. Until district Annual Financial Reports separate the line, “districts are becoming vendors” is a behavioural claim and not a financial one.

Florida's Step Up For Students operates a Contracted Public Schools channel that lets districts and charter schools sell part-time services — courses, tutoring, therapy, assessments — directly to scholarship families, paid from scholarship funds. One administrative detail makes it work: a student receiving contracted services is not considered enrolled in the public school for scholarship-eligibility purposes. A district can sell instruction to a child it does not enroll and does not count.

The adoption curve is dated and public. Roughly one in three of Florida's 67 districts by the August 2025 school-year start. More than half by October 2025, including Miami-Dade, Orange, Hillsborough and Duval. Fifty of 67 approved as providers by April 2026. About 75% by May 2026, with 52 partnered including Hillsborough, Pinellas and Pasco. Fifty-three approved or in process by July 2026. Miami-Dade opened more than 95 classes to students not enrolled in the district.

The surrounding context is a state where roughly 53% of K-12 students — about 1.9 million children — use an education option other than their assigned district school, and where districts are closing buildings. Orange County closed seven schools at the end of 2025-26 after a single-year enrollment decline of roughly 6,600 to 7,000 students, redirected $211 million to scholarships in 2025-26 against $152 million the prior year, and will open no new campuses until 2031 after opening 28 in ten years. Broward is down about 37,000 students over a decade. Escambia projected losing about 7,000 students to scholarships heading into 2026-27.

The behaviour is not universal, and the exceptions are what give it meaning. Texas has paid districts a Foundation School Program allotment of $1,500 per University Interscholastic League activity for each participating non-enrolled homeschool student since 2023. Under the original opt-in rule, 45 districts participated in 2024-25 — about 4% of districts statewide. When a 2025 law flipped the default to automatic participation, Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington and Katy opted out anyway. A Katy trustee's stated reason was that non-district students participating could take opportunities away from enrolled students.

West Virginia is a third case. Its Hope Scholarship pays every student the same base amount regardless of setting, and state law lists individual classes and extracurricular activities provided by a public school district among qualifying expenses. Joining as a provider is free. Reading the state's participating-provider directory as of 10 August 2026, we found no county school district listed across the school block from roughly M through Y. That is a near-zero, not a verified zero. The directory's search function could not be queried programmatically, and a district could in principle be registered elsewhere in the list. We record it as unfinished rather than settled.

Three states, three outcomes, and the variation tracks policy design rather than district disposition. Florida pays the same amount regardless of setting, permits sales to non-enrolled students, and has a scholarship funding organisation actively recruiting districts as providers. Texas tiers its homeschool award far below its private-school award. West Virginia has both the funding parity and the statutory permission but, as far as we can find, no organisation selling districts on selling.

Why this sits in a postsecondary index. Districts in one state have spent a year learning to price, list and staff part-time instruction for families they do not enroll. That is new work, and someone is preparing the people who do it. This note records the demand. It does not yet identify the supply.

notes.title: In much of the Americas, the money follows the teacher
notes.standfirst: Coding North and South America turned up a mechanism the school-choice literature barely names: public money paid not per pupil, but against a private school's teaching payroll. Five systems in this hemisphere work that way.
body: The Atlas now codes every country in North and South America. The expected finding was a spread from Chile's voucher to Cuba's monopoly, and that spread is there. The unexpected finding is what sits in the middle.

Argentina subsidises private schools as a percentage of teachers' salary costs. Fee-free schools run by non-profit entities can receive up to 100%; fee-charging schools are banded at 80%, 60% or 40%. To be paid, a school submits its teaching payroll — staff, posts, hours, salaries — to the education authority. Just over 70% of private schools receive it, covering about 22% of all Argentine students.

Ecuador runs fiscomisional schools: religious schools holding a government agreement, subsidised specifically to pay teacher salaries. Belize funds denominational and community grant-aided schools — about 62% of all institutions — through direct payment of teachers' salaries, and from 2024 covers 100% of salaries, pensions and benefits for 879 grant-aided secondary and tertiary staff. Trinidad and Tobago has paid salaries at denominational schools since the Concordat of 1960, sixty-six years, while the denominations retain ownership, management and a right to request a teacher's removal on moral or religious grounds. French Guiana, as a French département, sits under the 1959 Loi Debré, where schools under contract teach the national programme and the state pays their teachers.
Five systems, one mechanism, and it is not a voucher. The unit of funding is a teaching post, not a pupil.

That distinction is not cosmetic, and it cuts directly at the question this organisation exists to ask. A voucher moves money and leaves the labour market to sort itself out — which is how the United States arrived at 750,000 children in microschools and 34% of teachers feeling prepared to teach in one. A payroll subsidy puts the workforce inside the funding formula. The state that writes the cheque for the teacher holds a lever on who may teach, whoever owns the school.

We are not claiming the payroll model performs better. Nobody has run that comparison, which is the point. The demand-side literature measures what families do with vouchers in exhaustive detail; there is no comparable body of work on what happens to teacher supply, preparation and credentialing under salary-side subsidy, despite Trinidad having run one for sixty-six years and Belize for longer.

Two more things the region gave up. Bolivia kept church-run schools and nationalised teacher preparation outright — Law 070 of 2010 made the State solely responsible for producing new teachers, and the Catholic training institute Sedes Sapientiae was closed. Guyana went the other way in 1976, taking close to 696 church and private schools into state control, and the stated justification was a staffing question: the churches had held major influence over who taught in their schools. Both countries legislated about who is permitted to make and place teachers. Neither measured what happened next.

The limit. Six countries — Honduras, Nicaragua, the Bahamas, Suriname, Greenland and the Falkland Islands — are shortlisted rather than coded, each with a stated reason on its panel. Suriname is the one to watch: it inherited the Dutch bijzonder onderwijs model, which would make it a direct sibling of the Netherlands entry, and no Surinamese source was located in this pass.

notes.title: Florida built a second door, and we walked past it
notes.standfirst: A 2021 law let Florida colleges sponsor charter schools. Four institutions now do. We had coded one of them "nothing found" — because we read its course roster and stopped.
body: Florida is the state this Index covers most heavily, and the state whose headline finding is the starkest: the most portable education money in America, and not one education-school program built for the sector it funds. That finding still stands.

What we missed is that a second pathway opened alongside it. A 2021 statutory change let Florida College System institutions sponsor charter schools within their service areas, and state universities sponsor them statewide. Four Florida institutions are now approved sponsors: Tallahassee State College, first approved in January 2023, which went on to open the first college-sponsored charter school in the state; Miami Dade College, whose board approved its first six charter applications in February 2026; Pasco-Hernando State College, which issued its first charter to a school that had spent a decade under the Pasco County school board; and the University of West Florida.

Miami Dade College went furthest. It does not merely sponsor — it powers the Florida Charter Institute, whose authorizing division reviews applications and conducts oversight on behalf of other higher-education authorizers, Pasco-Hernando among them. One college now runs the apparatus the others use.
Every one of these moves happens outside the college of education. That is the same pattern the Index found in Michigan, in Arizona and in Indiana, and it is the pattern the Index was built to catch.

Which makes our error the point of this note. We coded the University of West Florida Tier 0 — nothing found — on the strength of its School of Education roster, which contains nothing built for the sector. UWF is listed as an approved sponsor in the Florida Department of Education's own directory, and its trustees approved it as authorizer of a Somerset Academy charter school. We made the catalog-scan mistake that this Index exists to correct, in our best-covered state.

The row is recoded and Correction 02 is permanent. The method has changed too: for every state, the official sponsor or authorizer registry is now checked before any institution can be coded Tier 0. That one change is what surfaced Miami Dade and Pasco-Hernando.

The limit worth carrying. Twenty-five Florida state colleges are not sponsors and their education units remain unscanned. A college can build a program without ever holding a charter, so the coverage gap has narrowed and changed shape rather than closed. And for Miami Dade and Pasco-Hernando, this note codes the authorizing move only — neither education unit has been enumerated to our standard, and we make no claim about their teaching programs in either direction.

notes.title: The program that was built and stopped
notes.standfirst: Every other null in the Index records an institution that never built for this sector. Nova Southeastern built one and no longer offers it — documented in the university's own archive.
body: The WMFC Readiness Index codes 14 institutions Tier 0 — nothing found. Until now every one of them meant the same thing: this education unit has not built anything for the portable-funding sector. Nova Southeastern University means something different.

NSUWorks, NSU's own institutional repository, holds a Program Overview titled NSU Master's Degree in Charter School Education/Leadership, attributed to the Fischler Graduate School of Education and Human Services and indexed under keywords including charter school, Miami-Dade, specialization and modified core. It is a real program document, deposited by the university.

The current master's roster of the Abraham S. Fischler College of Education & School of Criminal Justice was read in full on 8 August 2026. It offers Applied Behavior Analysis, Child Protection, Criminal Justice, Developmental Disabilities, Education, Educational Leadership and Leadership. There is no charter or choice-sector program.

What we cannot say. The repository dates the document only approximately — 2002, deposited 2016 — and holds no discontinuation record. We can document that the program existed and that it is now absent. We cannot say when it ended, and no one should cite a year. We had published this as an unproven suspicion since July; it is now proven in one direction and still open in the other.

Why the distinction matters. The Index offers four competing explanations for why education colleges have built so little. Every one of them is a theory about non-construction. A program that was built and did not survive is a different event, and it points at questions none of the four currently ask: who bought it, how many, and what stopped.

notes.title: Eight authorizers, one program
notes.standfirst: Michigan is the deepest university-charter ecosystem in the country. All eight public university authorizers are now coded. Between them they hold well over 200 schools and exactly one preparation program.
body: The working hypothesis was simple and testable: universities build for this sector when they hold schools in it. Michigan was the place to test it, because Michigan universities have chartered schools since 1994 and eight of them still do.

Six were unexamined until this edition — Oakland, Saginaw Valley State, Northern Michigan, Eastern Michigan, Ferris State and Lake Superior State. All six are now coded. None has built a preparation program for the sector. Central Michigan's Charter School Leadership M.A. remains the only one in a scan of 39 institutions.

The result is not that nothing happens. Three of the six reach the education college directly, and each does it in a different way. Oakland University houses its Office of Public School Academies inside the School of Education and Human Services and states the reason plainly — the placement exists “marshalling the strength of its programs and faculty to increase the proficiency and expertise of Academy teachers and administrators.” Its leadership degrees still prepare principals and deans of students, with no charter or choice content. Saginaw Valley State gives teachers and administrators of its 17 academies 50–75% tuition remission to complete a College of Education program — a change in the price of the standard degree, not in its contents. Northern Michigan describes its nine academies as providing “hands-on classroom experience for NMU's hundreds of elementary and secondary education majors” — the charter schools are practicum sites feeding conventional licensure.
Proximity, subsidy and access were each present. None produced a program.

The hypothesis does not survive in its simple form. Scale does not rescue it either: Grand Valley State holds 78 schools and more than 34,000 students, more than Central Michigan, and has built no degree. Holding schools, holding many schools, and holding them inside the education college were all insufficient.

That leaves a sharper question than the one we started with. Michigan is complete and the answer is no. The open problem is no longer whether the Central Michigan pattern repeats — it does not — but why it happened once.

notes.title: Nobody owns the workforce question
notes.standfirst: Demand is measured. Policy adoption is measured. Preparation quality is measured. Whether the workforce exists to staff what policy enables falls between every organization in the field.
body: The organizations working in this space each measure their own side of the ledger, and measure it well. EdChoice counts families, programs and fiscal effects. ExcelinEd tracks policy adoption across some forty areas. NCTQ measures the quality of teacher preparation. NACSA tracks authorizers. AACTE represents and advocates for the preparation pipeline.
Put those five together and one question still has no owner: as public money becomes portable, does the educator workforce exist to staff what the policy has enabled?

It is nobody's failure. Each organization is doing its own job, and the question sits outside all of their remits — it requires demand-side data from one, policy data from another, and institution-level observation that none of them collects. It falls in the seam.
WMFC exists to occupy that seam. This is not a criticism of the field; it is the reason there is room for another instrument in it.

notes.title: Where universities engage, they operate
notes.standfirst: Most confirmed university entries into the choice sector took the form of running or authorizing a school rather than building a degree. A catalog scan would miss all of them.
body: The obvious way to ask whether education colleges have responded to portable funding is to search their course catalogs. It is also the way to get the wrong answer.

Across the states examined, the confirmed university entries into this sector are overwhelmingly operating moves — running a school, or holding the charter for one. Arizona State operates schools. Indiana University East engages through its region's charter environment. Florida's universities hold lab-school charter authority, and both UF and FSU run lab schools. Michigan's eight public university authorizers hold hundreds of schools between them.
None of that appears in a course listing. An institution can be deeply committed to this sector, in public, at scale, for thirty years, and register as a null in any catalog-based scan.

This is the methodological difference the Readiness Index is built around: operating and authorizing moves are coded, not just programs. Both are institutional responses. Counting only one of them produces a picture that is not merely incomplete but backwards — it makes the most engaged institutions look like the least.

notes.title: The 53-point preparedness cliff
notes.standfirst: 87% of teachers feel prepared to teach in a district school. 34% feel prepared for a microschool — the sector now serving more than 750,000 children.
body: Teachers were asked how prepared they felt to teach in each kind of school. The answers fall in a straight line away from the model their preparation was built around:
Public district 87% · Private 74% · Charter 67% · Religious 49% · Microschools 34%.

The gap between the first and the last is 53 points. It is not a gap between good schools and bad ones; it is a gap between the setting preparation programs are designed for and the setting growing fastest.

Two things make the number worse than it looks. More than 70% of the people running microschools are current or former licensed teachers — these are not outsiders to the profession, they are its own graduates reporting that their training did not cover where they went. And the figure has not moved since 2023.

The data is EdChoice's own. That matters: the organization that most consistently documents the demand side published the clearest available statement of the supply-side problem, and the field has not yet answered it.
